title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 18
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A government introduced automatic enrolment in workplace pensions, with employees free to opt out, and reports that participation rose from 45 per cent to 85 per cent. Officials conclude that most employees had wanted to save for retirement but had not got round to enrolling.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the officials' conclusion?
options: A. Employers contribute to enrolled employees' pensions.
B. Opting out requires a written request.
C. Participation rose fastest among younger workers.
D. Surveys of the newly enrolled find that a large share are unaware they are enrolled, and their contributions have not displaced any other saving.
E. Some employees enrolled before the change.
questions.explanation: Inattention explains the take-up as readily as latent desire; if people do not know they are enrolled, the outcome reveals the power of the default rather than a preference.

questions.prompt: An ambulance service reports that its average response time has fallen from nine minutes to seven. Managers conclude that patients are now reached more quickly.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. The service purchased additional vehicles.
B. Traffic congestion has worsened in the area.
C. The service reclassified many urgent calls into a category whose response times are recorded separately and are not included in the average.
D. Response times are measured from the moment a vehicle is dispatched.
E. The service covers a large rural area.
questions.explanation: Moving slow cases out of the measured category lowers the average without reaching anyone faster. D is a real definitional weakness but was true before and after.

questions.prompt: A farm advertises its vegetables as pesticide-free, citing that no synthetic pesticide has been applied to its fields for three years.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the advertisement's implied claim about the produce?
options: A. Testing finds pesticide residues on the farm's produce at levels similar to conventional produce, carried by spray drift from neighbouring fields.
B. Organic certification requires four years without synthetic pesticide.
C. The farm uses mechanical weeding instead.
D. Some customers prefer local produce regardless of method.
E. The farm's yields are lower than the regional average.
questions.explanation: The claim about practice may be true while the claim consumers hear — about what is on the vegetables — is not. A concerns a labelling standard rather than the produce.

questions.prompt: A telephone manufacturer notes that customers who buy its screen protectors report cracked screens less often, and advertises the protector as preventing screen damage.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the advertisement?
options: A. How much the protectors cost
B. Whether customers who buy protectors also use protective cases and handle their telephones more carefully
C. Whether the protectors are made of glass or plastic
D. How many colours the telephone is available in
E. Whether the manufacturer sells cases as well
questions.explanation: Protector buyers are likely to differ in other protective behaviour, so the comparison may reflect the customer rather than the product.

questions.prompt: Every dish on the Halloway staff canteen menu that is prepared on site is priced below three pounds. No dish priced below three pounds contains imported seafood. Some dishes on the menu contain imported seafood.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Dishes prepared on site are cheaper to produce.
B. Most dishes are prepared on site.
C. No dish on the menu costs more than three pounds.
D. Imported seafood is more expensive than local seafood.
E. Some dishes on the menu are not prepared on site.
questions.explanation: Seafood dishes are not under three pounds, and on-site preparation implies that price, so those dishes are not prepared on site. B and E introduce cost claims the statements do not make.

questions.prompt: A cinema chain introduced a loyalty card and reports that cardholders visit more often than non-cardholders. It plans to issue cards to all customers automatically in order to raise attendance.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
options: A. Cards are free to issue.
B. Customers apply for the card when they expect to visit frequently enough to earn its rewards.
C. Some cardholders visit only at weekends.
D. The chain operates in twelve cities.
E. Attendance is highest during school holidays.
questions.explanation: The card marks an intention that already exists; issuing it to everyone cannot manufacture the intention that made cardholders frequent visitors.

questions.prompt: A forestry agency thinned a dense plantation and reports that the remaining trees grew faster in the following years. It concludes that thinning increases the productivity of a plantation.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion as stated?
options: A. Thinning is expensive to carry out.
B. Thinned stands are less prone to disease.
C. The thinned trees were sold for pulp.
D. Total timber volume across the stand grew more slowly after thinning than before, since the faster growth of individual trees did not compensate for the trees removed.
E. Growth rates vary with rainfall.
questions.explanation: Per-tree growth and stand productivity are different quantities, and the conclusion is stated in terms of the plantation. C and D describe other benefits without addressing it.

questions.prompt: A tourism board argues that hotel star ratings should be replaced by guest review scores, since reviews reflect the experience of actual guests rather than an inspector's checklist.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the board's argument?
options: A. Some hotels dispute their star ratings.
B. Inspections are carried out annually.
C. Review scores rate a hotel against the guest's expectations, so a modest hotel that is exactly as described scores higher than a luxury hotel with a minor fault.
D. Reviews can be submitted only by verified guests.
E. Star criteria differ between countries.
questions.explanation: If the two systems measure different things — conformity to expectation against absolute facilities — replacing one with the other loses information travellers use, rather than improving the same measure.

questions.prompt: A rail operator installed wireless internet on its trains and reports that passenger numbers rose on the equipped routes. It concludes that onboard internet attracts passengers.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
options: A. The internet is free to use.
B. Passengers report that the connection is fast.
C. The operator also refurbished several stations.
D. Rail travel rose nationally that year.
E. The equipped routes were selected by drawing lots among routes with similar passenger trends, and numbers on the unequipped routes were flat over the same period.
questions.explanation: Random allocation among similar routes plus a flat comparison group removes the selection and the national-trend explanations at once.

questions.prompt: A school introduced free instrumental music lessons and reports that pupils taking them achieve higher marks in mathematics than pupils who do not. A local newspaper reports that music lessons improve mathematical ability.
questions.question: The newspaper's report is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. assumes that lessons taken voluntarily by particular pupils caused a difference that may reflect who chose them
B. does not specify which instruments were taught
C. ignores the cost of employing music teachers
D. relies on a single school's results
E. overlooks pupils who learn instruments privately
questions.explanation: Free lessons still require a pupil and family to opt in, and the disposition that produces that choice plausibly produces the mathematics marks as well.

questions.prompt: Supporters of a proposal to lower the speed limit on a rural road argue that it will reduce fatal collisions. Opponents reply that most collisions on the road involve drivers already exceeding the current limit.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the opponents' reply?
options: A. The road carries heavy goods vehicles.
B. Enforcement cameras are expensive.
C. Where limits have been lowered on comparable roads, average speeds fell among all drivers, including those who continued to exceed the limit.
D. Some drivers are unaware of the current limit.
E. The road has several sharp bends.
questions.explanation: The reply assumes law-breakers are unaffected by the limit; evidence that the whole speed distribution shifts, including its upper tail, removes that assumption.

questions.passageText:
A manufacturer that sets a minimum price at which its product may be resold is restricting competition among its own retailers, and for most of the twentieth century such arrangements were treated as almost automatically unlawful. The economic case against them is straightforward: prices are higher than they would otherwise be, and the practice can serve as cover for a cartel among either manufacturers or retailers.

There is a competing account, and it is not merely an apologia. Some products sell better when a retailer provides services — demonstration, advice, trained staff, stock held for inspection — that cost money to supply. A customer can take the advice in one shop and buy from a discounter that provides none, and a retailer who anticipates this will not provide the service. A price floor removes the discounter's advantage and makes the service sustainable, which is why the practice appears disproportionately with products that reward pre-sale explanation.

Distinguishing the two cases in a particular market is the difficulty. Both predict higher retail prices; only one predicts increased provision of service, and service is not easily measured. Courts asked to decide have generally lacked the evidence to separate them, which is an argument about institutional capacity rather than about economics.

The regulatory position has shifted from prohibition toward case-by-case assessment. That is defensible in principle and expensive in practice, and it has the characteristic weakness of any standard that requires proof: the party with the better information about whether service actually increased is the party whose conduct is under examination.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the economic case against resale price maintenance includes that it
options: A. reduces the number of retailers in a market
B. can serve as cover for a cartel among manufacturers or retailers
C. prevents manufacturers from advertising
D. lowers the quality of the products sold
E. makes retail service unprofitable
questions.explanation: Higher prices and the cartel-cover concern are the two elements named. E states the opposite of the competing account.

questions.passageText:
A forager honeybee returning to the hive performs a repetitive movement on the comb, and von Frisch proposed that its orientation and duration encode the direction and distance of a food source. The claim is now in textbooks. Its acceptance took decades, and the reason is worth understanding.

The original evidence was correlational: the dance varied systematically with the location of the feeder, and recruits arrived at the feeder in numbers. A critic pointed out that both facts are consistent with a simpler explanation in which recruits find the food by odour carried on the dancer or released at the site, with the dance serving only to arouse them. The correlation between dance and location would then be real but causally idle.

Settling this required interventions rather than observations. Experiments using a mechanical bee that performed dances without any accompanying odour recruited bees to the indicated location, though less efficiently than a live dancer. Displacement experiments moved recruits after they had watched a dance and found their search centred where the dance had indicated rather than where odour would lead. And radar tracking of individual recruits showed flight paths consistent with the vector the dance specified.

The modern position is not that the critic was wrong about odour, which does matter, but that the dance conveys information in addition to it. What the episode illustrates is how much work is required to move from a correlation that everyone can see to a causal claim about what an animal communicates, and how a plausible simpler explanation deserves the effort of being excluded rather than dismissed.
questions.prompt: The critic's alternative explanation described in the passage held that recruits found food
options: A. by odour carried on the dancer or released at the site, with the dance merely arousing them
B. by following the dancer in flight
C. by memory of previous foraging
D. by observing the sun's position
E. at random, in proportion to the food available
questions.explanation: The point of the objection is that the dance-location correlation could be real but causally idle.

questions.passageText:
Few questions in education research have absorbed more effort than the effect of class size on attainment, and the literature's shape is instructive about how evidence accumulates in a politically charged field.

Observational studies were long inconclusive, and for a reason that should have been obvious: class sizes are not assigned at random. Struggling pupils are placed in smaller groups, so the raw association between small classes and poor outcomes runs opposite to any causal effect, while wealthier schools with smaller classes generate an association running the other way.

The best evidence comes from designs that break the link between class size and pupil characteristics. A large randomised experiment in the United States assigned pupils and teachers to classes of different sizes in the early grades and found gains for the smaller classes, larger for disadvantaged pupils, and partly persistent afterwards. Studies exploiting rules that force a class to split once it exceeds a threshold have found effects in the same direction, generally smaller.

The complication is cost. Reducing class size across a system requires many additional teachers, and where the supply of good teachers is limited, the marginal recruit may be enough worse than the average to offset the benefit of the smaller group. That interaction is rarely captured in a study of a single school and is precisely what a system-wide policy would encounter. The honest summary is that smaller classes help, most where pupils are most disadvantaged, and that whether reducing them is the best use of the money is a different question the class-size literature cannot answer.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, observational studies of class size were inconclusive because
options: A. attainment is difficult to measure
B. schools do not record class sizes accurately
C. teachers vary in quality
D. the effects appear only years later
E. class sizes are not assigned at random, and the selection runs in both directions
questions.explanation: Struggling pupils placed in smaller groups and wealthier schools with smaller classes generate associations of opposite sign.

questions.passageText:
The idea that a text belongs to the person who composed it, and that this ownership is the natural basis of literary property, is younger than it appears. For most of the history of writing, texts circulated with weak and variable attribution, and the interests protected by early printing privileges were those of printers rather than writers.

The modern conception assembled itself in the eighteenth century, out of a legal argument and an aesthetic one that reinforced each other. Publishers seeking perpetual rights argued that a work was the product of an author's individual genius and therefore property in the fullest sense — an argument that served the publishers, since the rights they wanted were the ones they had bought from authors. Simultaneously, criticism was moving from valuing a work's fidelity to inherited models toward valuing originality, which gave the legal argument its cultural support.

The consequences run deeper than the term of copyright. A conception of writing as individual creation fits some kinds of work badly: collaborative composition, oral traditions with no identifiable originator, translation and editing, and the accumulation of scientific results. Legal systems have handled these by treating them as exceptions to a norm rather than as evidence that the norm describes a subset of how texts are made.

Recognising the concept's history is not an argument for abolishing it. It is a reason to treat questions about who owns a text as questions about which arrangement produces the work we want, rather than as deductions from a natural fact about creation.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that early printing privileges protected the interests of
options: A. printers
B. authors
C. readers
D. translators
E. the state exclusively
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph, alongside the observation that attribution itself was weak and variable.

The honest summary is that smaller classes help, most where pupils are most disadvantaged, and that whether reducing them is the best use of the money is a different question the class-size literature cannot answer.

readingPassages.title: Inventing the Author
readingPassages.text:
The idea that a text belongs to the person who composed it, and that this ownership is the natural basis of literary property, is younger than it appears. For most of the history of writing, texts circulated with weak and variable attribution, and the interests protected by early printing privileges were those of printers rather than writers.

The modern conception assembled itself in the eighteenth century, out of a legal argument and an aesthetic one that reinforced each other. Publishers seeking perpetual rights argued that a work was the product of an author's individual genius and therefore property in the fullest sense — an argument that served the publishers, since the rights they wanted were the ones they had bought from authors. Simultaneously, criticism was moving from valuing a work's fidelity to inherited models toward valuing originality, which gave the legal argument its cultural support.

The consequences run deeper than the term of copyright. A conception of writing as individual creation fits some kinds of work badly: collaborative composition, oral traditions with no identifiable originator, translation and editing, and the accumulation of scientific results. Legal systems have handled these by treating them as exceptions to a norm rather than as evidence that the norm describes a subset of how texts are made.

Recognising the concept's history is not an argument for abolishing it. It is a reason to treat questions about who owns a text as questions about which arrangement produces the work we want, rather than as deductions from a natural fact about creation.
